title: Older woman neglected by her son, neighbour reports (synthetic)
setting: A care assessor visits Edith Marsh, 84, at home at 6 Cobb Lane, Harbridge, for a needs assessment; her son Gary, her carer, is at work, and her neighbour Pauline Reid sits in at Edith's request.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Hello Mrs Marsh, I'm Janet, the care assessor from the council. We spoke on the phone.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Oh yes, come in, love. This is Pauline from next door, I asked her to sit with me. My hearing's not great.

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: Hiya. I hope that's alright.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Of course, if Mrs Marsh wants you here. Is it Edith or Mrs Marsh?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Edith's fine.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Lovely. So Edith, today I'm here to find out what help you need at home. I'll write notes. It's confidential, but if I'm worried about your safety I might need to share information with others, like your GP. Is that okay?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes, that's alright.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Let's start with getting about. How are you on your feet?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I use my frame. I don't go upstairs now, Gary brought my bed down to the front room.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: That's Gary, your son?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes, he lives with me. He looks after me. He works at the garage on Station Road.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: What hours does he work?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Eight till six, I think. Sometimes later.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: And what does Gary help you with?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: He does my shopping, and gets me up. And my tablets.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay. Can you get to the toilet yourself?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Mostly. I've got a commode. I'm not always quick enough, I wear the pads.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: That's really common, Edith, no need to be embarrassed. Who helps you change if the pad's wet?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Gary does, when he's home. Or I manage.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: So during the day, while Gary's at work, is anyone else here?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Well. Not really. I'm, um. I'm alone all day. But I'm alright, I have the telly.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: From when Gary goes to work?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: He goes about half seven. Sometimes he doesn't get back till nine. He's ever so busy. He does his best.

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: Can I say something, Edith? I'm not trying to cause trouble.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Go on, then.

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: I pop in most afternoons. And most days she's left in wet clothes, all day. The pad and her skirt are wet when I come in at two.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Most days?

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: Four or five days a week, I'd say. I help her change if she'll let me.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Thank you, Pauline. Edith, is that right?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Sometimes. I don't like to make a fuss for Gary.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: What about food, Edith, what do you have for lunch?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Gary leaves me a sandwich. Usually.

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: There's no food in the fridge, though. On Saturday I looked, there was no food in the fridge at all, just a bit of milk gone off. I brought her a dinner round.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Is that usual, Pauline?

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: The last few weeks, yes. It's been empty three or four times when I've looked.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay. And you mentioned tablets. Gary does your tablets?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: He puts them out. In the box.

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: The box is on the side there. She's not had her tablets for a week. It's full since last Tuesday, look, all the days.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Can I have a look, Edith?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes, go on.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay, so the compartments from Tuesday the seventeenth onwards are all still full. That's her blood pressure tablet and the water tablet, it says.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I forget. And Gary's been busy.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: That's alright. Thank you for letting me look. Edith, I ask everyone this. Has Gary, or anyone, ever hit you or hurt you?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: No! Gary's never hit me. Never. He's a good boy, he's just tired.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay, thank you. Pauline, have you ever seen anything like that?

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: No, nothing like that. He's not unkind to her. He just isn't here.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay. Edith, what would you like? Do you want to stay living here?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Oh yes. I've been here since 1962. I don't want a home.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: That's really clear. Would you accept carers coming in, so you're not relying on Gary all day?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: If Gary doesn't mind. I don't want him upset.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: I'd like to talk to Gary as well. He's entitled to a carer's assessment, so he gets support too. Is that okay?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes. He'd like that, I think. He's struggling.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: And money, do you get your pension paid into your own account?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes, and Gary takes some out for the shopping. I've got my card.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Do you get Attendance Allowance?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I don't think so. What's that?

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: She doesn't, I asked Gary once.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: It's a benefit for people who need care, it might be worth about seventy pounds a week. We can help you apply.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Oh, that'd help.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: So, here's the plan. I'm worried about you being left wet, without food and without your tablets, so I'm going to raise a safeguarding concern today. That's so we can get support in quickly, not to get Gary into trouble. Are you okay with that?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: If it helps Gary. Yes.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Today I'll ring your GP, Dr Patel, about the missed tablets, and ask the chemist about a blister pack and a check. I'll also arrange an emergency home care package, two calls a day, to start by Friday the twenty-seventh.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Two calls?

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Morning and lunchtime, for washing, changing and a meal. I'll phone Gary tonight and book his carer's assessment for next week.

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: I can keep popping in, I don't mind.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: That's really kind, Pauline. Can I take your number in case I need to check something?

lines.speaker: S3
lines.text: Course. It's oh one four six, I'll write it down.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Thanks. I'll come back on Wednesday the second of December with the Attendance Allowance form. Edith, anything else you'd like to ask?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: No, love. Thank you for coming.

disclosures.what: Pauline, the neighbour, says Edith is left in wet clothes all day on most days, four or five days a week.
must_keep: four or five days a week

disclosures.what: Pauline says there was no food in the fridge on Saturday, and it has been empty three or four times recently.
Pauline says Edith has not had her tablets for a week; the dosette box is full from last Tuesday.
Edith says she is alone all day, from about half seven until Gary gets back as late as nine, and is protective of her son.

controls.must_not_claim: Edith's son Gary has hit her.
